What is ?

is a state management system built around a deterministic, reactive pipeline. It combines the discipline of Redux-style state transitions with modern reactive programming to help applications manage state clearly, predictably, and at scale.

This page provides a high-level, plain-language explanation of what is, the problems it solves, and the mental model behind its core ideas.

TL;DR

is designed for applications that need clarity, composability, and confidence in how state changes over time.

  • Predictable, ordered state updates
  • Clear ownership boundaries per feature
  • Reactive consumption suitable for modern UIs
  • Extensibility without hidden side effects

By combining a disciplined update model with reactive output, provides a foundation that scales from small features to large applications.

Why Exists

was created in response to recurring pain points in real-world application state management—especially in large, long-lived JavaScript Framework applications where state tends to become fragmented, over-engineered, or difficult to reason about over time.

The goal was not to invent a new paradigm, but to remove friction while preserving the things that already work: predictability, explicit data flow, and strong boundaries.

The Core Motivations

  1. Remove Boilerplate
    Traditional state systems often require large amounts of repetitive setup—actions, reducers, selectors, effects—before any real business logic can be expressed. was designed so that state logic lives where it’s used, with minimal ceremony and no redundant scaffolding.
  2. Remove the Dispatch Mental Overhead
    Explicit dispatching introduces indirection that often obscures intent. replaces dispatch with direct, explicit state update APIs (replaceState, mergeState) that clearly express what is happening without hiding it behind event objects.
  3. Centralize Ownership Without Centralizing Everything
    Instead of one global store, centralizes ownership, not data. Each FeatureCell owns exactly one slice of state, with a clear lifecycle and responsibility, avoiding both global sprawl and excessive coupling. This supports large-scale application maintenance by promoting single-purpose features and modern, ownership-driven architectural practices.
  4. Treat State as a Stream
    Modern applications are inherently reactive. treats state changes as a continuous, deterministic stream flowing through a pipeline, rather than isolated mutations. This makes state easier to reason about over time, not just at a single moment.
  5. Fluent, Intent-Driven APIs
    Configuration and setup use a fluent API that reads like intent rather than configuration. The Vault is initialized using this fluent API directly alongside the feature code, allowing filters, reducers, callbacks, and behaviors to be declared in one place. This makes state behavior easier to compose, easier to review, and harder to misuse.
  6. Built-In, Layered Error Handling
    provides first-class error handling at both the feature and application levels. Errors can be handled directly within a FeatureCell when they are domain-specific, or observed globally through the VaultErrorService for centralized logging, monitoring, analytics, and tooling. This layered model is built in by default, requiring no custom error buses, global stores, or additional infrastructure.
  7. Make State Extensible by Design
    Real applications need persistence, encryption, caching, analytics, and debugging. bakes extensibility into the core through Behaviors, allowing capabilities to be added or removed without rewriting state logic or breaking contracts. This gives engineers a clear path to use built-in behaviors, adopt community-provided extensions, or author their own behaviors to meet evolving state management needs.

  8. is built with standard TypeScript primitives. There are no code generators, no hidden runtime tricks, and no opaque abstractions. What you write is what runs.
  9. Declarative, Not Implicit
    State behavior in is declared explicitly: what updates state, how it flows through the pipeline, and which behaviors participate. There are no hidden side effects or implicit execution paths.
  10. Modern Programming Techniques
    is built around modern concepts—immutability, composition, deterministic pipelines, and reactive primitives—without forcing developers to adopt unfamiliar or experimental syntax.
  11. Testability as a First-Class Concern
    Because FeatureCells are isolated, lifecycle-bound, and deterministic, state logic can be tested without global setup, mocking entire stores, or simulating complex event chains.
A Simple Analogy

A useful way to think about is to imagine a battery.

The Vault is the battery casing — secure, stable, and responsible for holding everything together. Each FeatureCell inside the Vault is like an individual battery cell, contributing its own energy (state) to the overall system.

Each FeatureCell focuses on its own responsibility, while the Vault ensures all cells work together in a coordinated, predictable way.

and

A Vault defines system-level runtime configuration used by FeatureCells, such as queue behavior and logging defaults. It serves as a shared configuration surface and coordination context, but does not expose FeatureCell initialization, state access, or state update APIs.

A FeatureCell is a feature-scoped State container and the primary consumer-facing API surface. It defines a single feature domain and exposes the entry points used to initialize state, read state, and apply updates through replaceState() and mergeState().

In practice, a FeatureCell represents one clearly owned slice of application state, with a well-defined lifecycle and a focused responsibility. This structure enables scalable, manageable state management by centralizing state ownership and behavior without introducing unnecessary coordination or boilerplate.

The Pipeline

All state updates in flow through a deterministic pipeline. Whether a FeatureCell replaces state or merges a partial update, the update is processed in a known order and produces a predictable result.

This pipeline-based approach ensures that transformations, side effects, persistence, and observation all happen in a consistent and inspectable way.

State and Snapshots

In , state is treated as immutable data owned by a FeatureCell. Rather than mutating state directly, updates are processed through the pipeline and emitted as new results.

These results are exposed as Snapshots — immutable representations of state at a specific moment in time. Snapshots are what consumers observe and render.

This separation makes it easier to reason about loading states, errors, and data availability without mixing concerns.

Built-In Error Handling

provides a first-class, built-in error handling model that works at both the feature level and the application level.

Errors can be handled directly within a FeatureCell when the error is specific to that feature’s domain, or observed globally through the VaultErrorService when errors need to be monitored, logged, visualized, or reacted to across the entire application.

This dual-level approach allows teams to keep feature-specific error logic close to the feature itself, while still enabling centralized error reporting, analytics, and tooling without additional wiring or custom infrastructure.

All error normalization, propagation, and exposure is built into the system by default. Developers do not need to create custom error buses, global stores, or cross-cutting services to achieve consistent error handling.

Built-In DevTools and Observability

includes first-class observability out of the box. A dedicated Chrome DevTools plugin allows engineers to inspect FeatureCells, observe state transitions, trace pipeline stages, and debug errors in real time—without adding any application code.

Under the hood, all monitoring is powered by the InsightService, which emits structured, lifecycle-aware events from the pipeline. This same service can be used to build custom monitors, internal dashboards, analytics pipelines, or logging integrations tailored to your organization’s needs.

Because monitoring is part of the core runtime—not an afterthought—developers get deep visibility into state behavior while keeping application code clean, explicit, and free of instrumentation concerns.

How do you pronounce ?

(pronounced S-D-U-X) stands for Streams + reDUx + eXtendable. It is a way of organizing application state so that updates flow through a predictable pipeline, producing consistent, observable results.

At a high level, treats state changes as intentional updates that are processed in order, rather than ad-hoc mutations scattered across an application. This makes it easier to reason about how state changes, how errors occur, and how data moves from services to the UI.
